source.title: Towards Neural Scaling Laws on Graphs
source.authors: Jing-Zhe Liu; Hai-Tao Mao; Zhi-Kai Chen; Tong Zhao; Neil Shah; Ji-Liang Tang

record.tranche_reason: The study tests graph-domain scaling laws and qualifies them: depth changes model-scaling curves, and sufficiently large models can depart from the fitted curve when data are limited.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own scaling experiments on supervised graph tasks, so these bear on V4, V5 and parts of V7. Cited language-model findings are not results of this study. Appendix I derives a compute-allocation relationship from assumed scaling forms, but does not empirically test an optimal parameter/data split. It does not test language-model pretraining loss, downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss, or extrapolation to runs orders of magnitude larger.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own model-size and data-size sweeps on supervised graph tasks (graph regression and classification, node classification, link prediction) and fits power-law forms. This is a new setting with direct results on V5. It also shows that the choice of data-volume metric changes fit quality, and that curves bend away from the power law at large model size on limited data, which bears on V7. Depth effects concern graph models, not language models, so they are recorded under fits_no_version rather than V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that saturating power-law forms describe model and data scaling on supervised graph tasks. Unlike in NLP and CV, depth changes model-scaling behaviour. Node or edge counts are better data metrics than graph counts and unify data scaling across graph, node and link tasks. In an appendix they add that model scaling can collapse on limited data, plausibly due to overfitting. They also note that node-classification model scaling showed no clear gains (Appendix J).
record.recipe_differences: This is a graph-domain study of supervised regression and classification, using graph-model width/depth sweeps and graph dataset subsampling. It does not reproduce language-model pretraining-loss experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Model depth changes the scaling curves and best-performing depth. Graph count versus node/edge count changes data-scaling fits and comparisons. Limited training data is associated with overfitting and scaling collapse; more data mitigates overfitting.

fits_no_version.finding: For GCN, GIN, SAT and GraphGPS on OGBG-PPA (and in Appendix E on REDDIT-MULTI-12K, MOLHIV and MOLPCBA), model-scaling curves differ by depth at matched parameter counts. The best depth varies by model. The effect persists when aggregation or feed-forward layers are varied separately.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: V4-analogue for graph models: at fixed parameter count, depth changes graph-model scaling curves substantially, unlike reports for language models.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the Third Learning on Graphs Conference (LoG 2024), PMLR 269
record.problems: The study notes that graph datasets are small relative to those in CV or NLP and limits its investigation to supervised graph learning. Several reported numerical fits are presented in figures. The text has an apparent discrepancy in Section 6 about whether node or edge count gives the better synthetic-data fit, and an inconsistent panel reference for Figure 8.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results left out. Appendix figures reporting further loss/overfitting curves on Code2, additional datasets, or node-count counterparts are not separately catalogued where they repeat the reported depth/collapse or data-metric findings.

untested.parts: Language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation of small-run fits to runs orders of magnitude larger. Model sizes span only about 10^4 to 10^8 parameters, and no held-out prediction is tested.
Compute-optimal allocation. Appendix I only derives N_opt and E_opt as power laws of compute from assumed forms, with no experiment.
Shape-insensitivity in language models. The graph depth results are not on that system kind.
Image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes. Graph pretraining and unsupervised learning are excluded by the authors. Compute scaling is not measured.
Downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss.
Comparison of published LM exponents, parameter-counting conventions, training schedules and fitting methods.

missing.what: Model scaling for node and link tasks. SEAL on OGBL-COLLAB gains clearly with hidden size, but GraphSAGE on OGBN-ARXIV shows no clear gain. This bears on V5.
Depth-dependent scaling curves for GCN and GIN on REDDIT-MULTI-12K, OGBG-MOLHIV and OGBG-MOLPCBA

record.verdict_notes: The measures are test MSE, accuracy, AP, ROC-AUC, Hits and MRR after supervised training, not pretraining loss. The R2 values are read from figure captions. There are internal inconsistencies: Section 6 credits the node count while Figure 6 shows edges; the Figure 8 panel references are swapped; the Figure 11 subcaptions name the wrong dataset. The study is not an original source. The tranche is changed from T5 to T3 because the paper mainly extends the laws to a new domain.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Whether fits on small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
No empirical compute-optimal split is measured. Appendix I derives a graph parameter/data relationship under assumed scaling forms; it does not test the claimed allocation trend experimentally.
The study varies depth and some layer types in selected graph models, but does not test every architecture detail or a wide range of model families at fixed parameter count.
Tests supervised graph tasks, not image/video modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, or other training regimes.
No relationship between pretraining loss and downstream performance is tested.
The study shows setup-dependent graph scaling and curve collapse, but does not compare published language-model exponents or systematically vary fitting methods and parameter-counting conventions.
